Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 32(2), I have the honour today to table, in both official languages, the first annual report to Parliament on the state of forestry in Canada.
In keeping with the commitment inherent in the new Forestry Act to monitor and to protect our environment, of which our forests are such an essential component, this report establishes a new era of national accountability for forest management and resources.
In receiving this document, Mr. Speaker, you will notice that the current economic status of the health of the forests are presented in a form which is easy to understand and which will provide the general public a basis on which to form an opinion so they can participate in the decision-making process regarding our forests in the future.

[Editor's Note: See today's Votes and Proceedings.]

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a privilege to present a petition on behalf of a large number of constituents from Kamloops and surrounding communities in British Columbia.
The petitioners state that whereas the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and private broadcasting stations are required by the Canadian Broadcasting Act to provide access to their broadcasting facilities to all Canadian citizens on an equitable and non-discriminatory basis, and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has failed to act in good faith on behalf of three separate requests made by a Canadian citizen to have his views directed and presented over its provincial and national broadcasting facilities in direct context, the petitioners then are calling upon the Government of Canada to demand that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and all private broadcasting stations in Canada provide access to their broadcasting facilities to all Canadian citizens, said access to be in direct context.

Mr. Speaker, once again I have the honour to rise in the House and present a petition on behalf of the young farmers of Lambton County who state that our Canadian citizens are being polluted by the ever-increasing automotive emissions and whereas ethanol can be produced from com, wheat, and barley and is a renewable resource, plants remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
They state that a minimum 3.2 per cent oxygen content in gasoline fuels should be mandatory and MMT should be banned.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and the privilege to present a petition signed by approximately 43 residents of Edmonton, Kingston, Calgary, Surrey, Stoney Plain, and Victoria. They have all petitioned Parliament to put Canada back on track and indicate their support for the NDP's plan to restore VIA Rail.
Government Orders GOODS AND SERVICES TAX

April 9, 1991

Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and privilege today to present two petitions, both of which have been cleared through the clerk of petitions pursuant to Standing Order 36.
The first petition is signed by 32 residents, principally from British Columbia but from other points as well. It calls on Parliament to reject the goods and services tax and to ensure that if and when there is broad public consensus on a sales tax measure to replace the manufacturers' sales tax, this reform not be an opportunity for the government to impose a massive tax grab. The point of course is that the opposition of the Canadian people to the goods and services tax has in no way diminished.

Mr. Speaker, my second petition which is signed by 120 residents, principally of Edmonton, calls on the House and I quote from the petition: "We need Petro-Canada to remain 100 per cent Canadian thereby keeping the money it makes in Canada". The petitioners call on the House to defeat or repeal, which would be the more appropriate choice at this point, Bill C-84, an act respecting the privatization of the National Petroleum Company of Canada, and keep Petro-Canada as a Crown corporation acting in the best interests of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, it is my pleasure to present this petition from a number of constituents in my riding. In the petition, they comment that they know the Senate was established in 1867 to represent the regions of Canada and to provide a medium for sober second thought and, whereas the Senate now performs no useful function, is completely partisan and has proven, after many efforts, to be impossible to reform, the petitioners, humbly pray and call upon Parliament to abolish the Senate outright.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by prefacing my remarks with something I had intended to say yesterday. I had intended to mention of the good work done by a committee of the House in 1982-83, a committee headed by Tom Lefebvre who is now a senator in the other place. It was a committee on parliamentary reform and did some very good work. Among other things, it established a firm calendar to operate under and it got rid of evening sittings of the
April 9, 1991

House. Both of those were very important to us. There was resistance to that change, but he did it. The committee persevered, the House accepted it and it has been good.
I want to make a point to my friend from Winnipeg Transcona. Not all of the recommendations of that particular committee were accepted, nor were all of the recommendations of the McGrath Commission accepted. Every time committees like this meet and bring proposals forward, some of them get accepted and there is a general trend line of improvement of the way the House operates.
I pay tribute to the Tom Lefebvre committee as well as the McGrath commission. I point out that we resisted change. Allan MacEachen, who was House Leader at the time, certainly resisted it, not because he was opposed to change, but because he would have to learn the rules all over again. He is like some lawyers; they are all in favour of legal reform until they realize they have to learn new statute law and build new case law. They then lose their zest for legal reform.
I want to make that point, sir. The member for Winnipeg Transcona was asking about when the government does things that are not part of the campaign promises. That is a legitimate question. He could have used better examples. He mentioned GST and free trade. Those were both prominent in the campaigns. The 1987 white paper on taxation, which was tabled in June of 1987, was debated for 15 months before we went into the campaign and debated during the campaign. Those people who were opposed to the GST are now helping the public to believe that the government had no mandate to bring it in. For that they have to answer to themselves because they are not being honest with the public on this.
There was plenty of debate and, believe me, I was on the griddle many a time on the campaign trail concerning it. Mike Cassidy, the former member from Ottawa Centre, spoke on that. For people who are opposed to the GST, to help perpetuate the notion that there was no mandate, are being a little bit politically dishonest. I need to say nothing about the free trade debate. However, there are cases that the member for Winnipeg could have mentioned. For example, issues come forward after the campaign is over, after the government is in office, which could not have been anticipated during the campaign. I think there is only one thing for the opposition to do and that is to make sure that the government, when it
Government Orders
attacks and tackles those issues, does it within the confines of its own philosophy.
For a government like ours to promote decentralization and privatization and then bring in a bill that would create new Crown corporations would be a little bit contradictory. I think we would be rightfully taken to task for that. So they need to keep us consistent with our philosophy. That is fair.
There is another issue that is more difficult to handle, and that is when a political party allows its real agenda to be hidden during a campaign. That is a problem. The public needs to protect the whole democratic process of an election campaign by grilling each of the parties on what its real agenda is. That is the purpose of an election campaign. We have to get away from allowing the party hacks of all parties determining the campaign by way of slogans rather than substance. That is where democracy begins. We must not be bamboozled in any campaign by the superficial sloganeering.
The second question the member for Winnipeg asked was about the whole committee process. He said: "Would it not be better when the McGrath commission asked that committees deal with a process that would allow us to deal in principle and substance debated beforehand". He is right. He is absolutely right.
This is a speech.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, I am simply trying to deal with his questions and I have done it. When we dealt with the Canada Pension Plan bill, the minister of health at that time submitted the bill in principle. The whips have a job to do to make sure that their party is properly represented in committee. If we as members do not fulfil our obligations to sit in committees when we are challenged to do so, when we have signed up for it, then that system falls apart and the whip

April 9, 1991
Government Orders
gets powers we do not want him to have. It is up to us to make the system work.
Finally, I would simply say that those committees that are aggressive get the resources they need to do the work and the rooms they need to do the work. Those that are passive and take direction lose that. Those that give direction get the resources and the committee rooms they want.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in this debate today. I suggest in some ways it is a very important debate in this House, because it deals with the changes the government has proposed to our rules.
I want to say at the outset that I find the government's method of proceeding in this way to be contrary to the traditions of this House. My experience is that in most cases where substantial changes to the rules have been proposed, the government has dealt through a committee of the House and got a report from the committee.
I can go back to the last major rule changes, first of all rising out of the McGrath committee report, which are the most recent, but they go back to 1969 when the changes were made that provided for the time allocation rules of this House.
The government acted first through a committee of the House which considered the proposed changes, made a report, and the government then acted on the report. If you check the historical precedent in 1969, you will see the government in fact moved a motion, but that was simply to the same effect as the committee's report, and that motion was moved and proposed in the House after the committee had completed a detailed study of the rules.
This time we have had the government say in House leaders' meetings that it had changes it would like to propose to the rules; here they are; tell us what you think. I submit that it is contrary to the past practice of this House. It has denied the opportunity for public input on the changes that are being proposed which fundamentally affect the way this House operates. This House is, after all, the public forum of this country where
citizens have the right to express their views through their representatives and, on occasion directly, in the committees.
The government is changing the rules of the game to suit its own political purposes. We in the opposition object to that change. The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, the House leader for the Official Opposition, detailed our objections to those rules very carefully yesterday.
I am not going to review the same ground, but I do want to make a comment on the general approach of the government and suggest that it has been wrong-headed from the start on this issue.
Having said that, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Peace River for the active role he played in the negotiation process that led to the resolution that was tabled in the House. I was happy to work with him in the course of those negotiations. I acknowledge that some of the very sensible suggestions that were put forward from this side were accepted by him and included in the rules. He amended some of the government's original proposals to make them better in my view for all Canadians, and also more palatable for the members of the opposition parties in this House.
I submit that in the end, he was unable or unwilling to go far enough in making changes to the proposals. We have therefore moved an amendment to those rules to delete the particularly odious provisions that are included in the package that was tabled before the House. I recognize the efforts he made and I am sorry that we are unable to achieve more agreement. Had there been an opportunity for committee discussion on these rule changes, I believe that greater agreement would have been obtained on all sides. I am sorry that has not taken place. I am sorry it was not agreeable to him and to his superior, the government House leader, that in fact a reference on this motion be made to a committee so that detailed study could proceed in that body.
The essential thrust of these rule changes is to limit debate in this House. The rules seek to do it in two ways, first, by making the House sit less, and second, by streamlining-and I use the word advisedly-the closure rules.
April 9, 1991

I am not going to run through all of the rule changes in detail, but the amendment we have moved, that deletes a series of the proposed changes, deletes the new scheduling arrangements. It deletes the provision in the rules proposed that limits to 15 minutes the opportunity to present petitions from the people of Canada in this House. We deleted the changes in the closure rule that restrict the hours of debate by a further three hours after closure has been imposed. It is one of the most Draconian closure rules in the British Commonwealth, and yet the government is seeking to cut off another three hours of debate.
We have objected to the further change in the time allocation rules which will save the government another day of debate and will enable it to force through legislation in something like five days in this House, not counting first reading. We have objected to the reductions and limitations on budget and throne speech debates and on borrowing bills. That is the thrust of the amendment that we have moved. We have suggested that all of those rather odious provisions be stricken from the package that the government has put before this House.
In some ways I suppose it is not surprising that the opposition has taken this view, but I must say I was shocked to hear the government House leader, or read of the government House leader's comments in respect of the rule changes the other day. In his speech yesterday afternoon, he was protesting the outrageous comments of the hon. member for Kamloops. Well, I think everyone in this House knows that the hon. member for Kamloops has a tendency to exaggerate, a tendency to hyperbole, and tends to blow things out of proportion. In other words, I think making a mountain out of a molehill is a commonplace for the hon. member for Kamloops, and I think everybody here knows that. Having said that, the government House leader I thought protested too much yesterday, especially having regard to what he said in the Globe and Mail on March 23.1 would like to quote the government House leader. I quote the article by Susan Delacourt:
Mr. Andre says the opposition's planned fight against the rule changes is just for the sake of appearances, since the three party leaders have been actively negotiating the changes since December.
I presume he meant by that that just because you have been negotiating means you somehow agree. I think the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond in his very able speech yesterday made it very clear that we did
Government Orders
not agree. This is pure pie in the sky rubbish coming from the government House leader. He ought to know better. He went on to say:
"They will battle for show, but they're glad we're going ahead with it," he said. The government hopes to have the changes approved by the time the Commons adjourns on Wednesday,-
That was of course several weeks ago:
-but is prepared to have MPs come back on April 8 if more time is needed to get approval."
Since we only started the debate yesterday, it is obvious that more time is in fact needed.
For the government House leader, having accused the member for Kamloops of being unfair in labelling these changes as Fascist or dictatorial, to suggest that somehow we are opposing these for the purpose of show is a bit far-fetched. In fact, I suggest that it was a most improper suggestion. He ought not to have made it. We are not opposing these for show. We are opposing these because we believe in practice and in theory that the changes are bad.
We believe that this country functions best when it has a strong and effective opposition. In fact, that was the view of the Conservative Party until very recently when its ideas of Parliament and its role and its importance changed dramatically. I am going to deal with what I think are the reasons for those changes a little later in my speech, but I want to talk first about their attitude to the importance of opposition, which they have done so well for so many years in Canada, particularly throughout this century.
After all, it is only since 1984 that we have had any Conservative government hold office for any length of time in the course of this century, since Borden's government collapsed in 1921. Nevertheless, their role as an effective opposition is well known. Now, having found that government is less comfortable, they have decided that perhaps oppositions should be muzzled and controlled. That is the purpose of the rule changes that are before us today.
I would like to read a quotation from the book, the leading work I suggest, on the Parliament of Canada by Charles Edward Selwyn Franks, one of my distinguished constituents, and a good friend of mine, and a former professor of mine, who wrote in his book, The Parliament of Canada, on page 5 the following about the functions of Parliament. I will not detail the first four, which I believe the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond in

April 9, 1991
Government Orders
his very able speech yesterday mentioned. I will simply read the other two. He said this:
There are two further functions of parliament which are so important that they deserve to be identified in their own right, though they might also be subsumed under the general rubric of making a government work. The first of these is the function of parliament as a recruiting and training ground for political leaders; the second is the function of political communication, where the processes of Parliamentaiy discussion, in Bagehot's terms, express the mind of the people, teach society, and inform both government and citizen of grievances and problems.
That exposition of the importance of an opposition in Parliament to inform the people and to express their grievances in Parliament is a deep rooted one in the British parliamentary tradition. Over the years governments have sought to curtail the rights of oppositions to present grievances and to argue their case. Governments resent oppositions that look like a government in waiting because it is perceived that all the weaknesses of the government are shown up by a skilful and competent opposition.
What this government is facing in this House is exactly that, a skilful and competent opposition. It is suffering in the polls as a result of that fact and so it is seeking to close down Parliament, shut the opposition up so it cannot present itself as a reasonable, sensible and viable alternative.
If any greater authority on the role of an opposition is needed, I do not think I could find one, other than looking beyond perhaps the most famous of all opposition leaders in this century, Mr. Diefenbaker.
He used to lead hon. members opposite when he was Prime Minister, but he was better known as Leader of the Opposition. He was a disastrous Prime Minister, but as Leader of the Opposition, everyone acknowledged his effectiveness.
I am sure that Mr. Stanfield would acknowledge his effectiveness because throughout the years that that gentleman had the honour of leading the Conservative Party of Canada, he was constantly overshadowed by the former leader, Mr. Diefenbaker.
I would like to quote from a little work called "John G. Diefenbaker: Those Things We Treasure". It is a little
book of his speeches. The unfortunate thing about the book is that it does not give the source. It is just a selection of speeches on freedom and in defence of our parliamentaiy heritage published by MacMillan of Canada.
I am sorry that it does not give the source because I am sure that the speeches were delivered in important places and would add weight to the veracity of the statements contained in them.
Are you filling in time?
I see the hon. member for Lanark-Car-leton is waking up. I am glad he is enjoying my speech.
Are you filling in time?

I am filling in a good deal of time. If the hon. member would pay attention to it, I think he would find that he might change this resolution and realize what a mistake the government is making in proceeding this way.
I will read from page 5 of the little work: "On the Role of an Opposition". I quote:
Only a strong and alert opposition can hope to check and control the excessive powers contrary to the Constitution that may be assumed or conferred upon governmental administration, the so-called bureaucracy.
Only an alert opposition can prevent the short-cuts through democratic procedures that cabinet ministers and bureaucrats frequently find attractive. It is only the opposition, functioning as a recognized part of parliamentary proceedings, that stands opposed to the degeneration of the governmental system into a form of arbitrary direction of public affairs by the executive and the bureaucracy.
Without it, minorities woul stand unprotected. Freedom would wither. Individual liberty would be in jeopardy. Unwarranted and oppressive invasion of private rights would grow unchecked.
Without an effective opposition, the administration in office could and would carry on the task of running the country under circumstances identical with the totalitarian one-party state. To some, this may seem an efficient way of running the country, but the first victim under such a regime as Hitler, Stalin and Mussolini demonstrated is freedom itself.
Without an opposition, it is not too much to say the parliamentary system of government would fail in its primary task of protecting the rights of individuals and minorities, and of ensuring freedom and democracy. In the parliamentary system, an opposition is as necessary as the cabinet itself. One without the other would mean tyranny or chaos.
April 9, 1991

It is commonplace that governments view an effective opposition as an obstruction. That is a view that is too often and too lightly taken up by unthinking critics of Parliament. An opposition that discharges its parliamentary responsibilities may appear in the superficial view to be obstructionist.
Extended opposition means lengthy debate. It was the British Labour Party chairman, Professor Harold Laski, who wrote that the alternative to the talking shop is the concentration camp.
I suggest that these words of the former Leader of the Conservative Party, the former Prime Minister of Canada and a distinguished Leader of the Opposition, are words that the government should be paying attention to.
It should follow the advice contained in Mr. Diefen-baker's words and heed them. I quote again from his works, on page 36 of this book:
Professor Ivor Jennings, the great English authority on Parliament said, and rightly, that the function of Parliament is not to govern but to criticize, to modify government policy and to educate public opinion.
To those who say that Parliament should be turning out legislation in quantify, my answer is that its mission is freedom and the assurance that all the people shall receive justice. It is not a slot machine into which one drops a slug to see the legislation come out.
I suggest that this government takes the attitude that Parliament is a sausage machine or a slot machine into which one drops a slug and watches legislation come out. The evidence of that is manifold throughout the list of changes that it has proposed to the Standing Orders.
I could quote further from the book, but like many of Mr. Diefenbaker's speeches, it is very repetitious.
I do commend hon. members, though, to read the work. I think they will find that instead of sitting there supporting this resolution they will stand up and admit that they are wrong, make changes in it and agree to the amendment that we have proposed in this House.
I would like to go back in time to 1969, because one of the changes this government is proposing to the Standing Orders is a change to the time allocation rules. Time allocation rules were brought in in this House in 1969 by the then Liberal government over the profound objections of the opposition. The hon. member for Peace River can correct me if I am wrong, but in 1969 there was no member in this House sitting on the Conservative benches who is currently sitting here. I believe all have moved on to greater things. Sorry, the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants was here. He is now an independent member. I can see he recanted from his views and has moved on to greater things. The government
Government Orders
finally used closure to get these rules through, after 12 days of debate. After 12 days of debate. I want to point that out to the parliamentary secretary. I can assure him that if closure is applied on this debate, he will hear about the 12 days of debate that went on in 1969. We are quite prepared to debate these for 12 days, I can assure the hon. member.
Pardon? The hon. member asks how many hours a day. I will get the information and check, but I assure him that it was very similar to the hours of sitting that we now have. Because, of course, there were night sittings in those days and they sat late and worked at night. Oh, this is a phoney point of order.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Point of order. Just on behalf of the government, we accept his offer to extend the sitting this evening so that more debate can occur, and I hope the unanimous feeling exists in the House.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's kind intervention. He knows it wasn't a point of order; it was just an attempt to disrupt my speech.
I wanted to read from Mr. Diefenbaker's speech on the occasion of the debate on these rule changes. What happened was that Mr. Diefenbaker and the members of his party-and at another time I may quote some of the other members-but the changes that were brought in by the time allocation motion were said to be a total disaster for Parliament. The Conservative Party at that time took the view that this was going to destroy the institution. We all know that somehow Parliament survived those changes and the rule has been used from time to time, although not extensively.
What Mr. Diefenbaker said on that occasion was this: "I ask this of the ministers-and I am faced by a galaxy of two, two ministers sitting across the corridor when Parliament is discussing a matter that, if carried into effect, will be the death sentence of this institution." I see I have one so he doubled that.
He went on to say: "They sit and they smirk." This is what Mr. Diefenbaker said about the attitude of the government to the rule changes that the government was proposing and that, in fact, have been used and adopted in this country for many years. This government, which used to say this was such a disaster, is now proposing to reduce the time available to members to discuss rule changes, even under the present time allocation rules. It is cutting by one day the time available for debate at

April 9, 1991
Government Orders
report and third reading stage as a result of these changes.
The hon. member looks surprised. Read the rules. It cuts it by 24 hours. I say that it is a shocking abuse of the government's authority in this House.
Why is the government flying in the face of these historical principles that give the opposition an opportunity to oppose?
I see that my time has run out, Mr. Speaker, so I am going to have to answer that question myself, either in questions and comments or in my next speech on the subamendment that I expect will be moved later.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Ten minutes, questions and comments period. The hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-South Langley.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I would just like to ask the member, who understands rules and procedure very well, why he chose to give us a history lesson instead of dealing with the technical difficulties he sees in the rule changes. Why would he do that when we are debating rule changes, and he does not deal with that?

The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond gave an extremely lucid and very clear exposition on the technical difficulties with the rule changes. Perhaps the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-South Langley did not understand when I said in my speech that I was not going to traverse the same territory he had. I have tried to explain the thrust of the the very technical rules. I did give a list that we are objecting to in our amendment. They are all being objected to because they cut the time available to members of the opposition to speak in this House and for this House to work through three methods: By shortening the times of sittings; by reducing the number of sitting days by about 41; and by reducing the number of days available to the opposition to debate the matters it chooses. There are five days taken away from us as supply days. There are two days taken away from the debate in reply to the speech from the throne, and there are two days taken off the budget debate. In addition to
that there is a two-day limitation on second reading of the borrowing bill.
All those are effectively opposition days. They are days when the opposition can choose to move amendments and debate subjects of its choosing, not subjects dictated by government order and decree.
What I am saying to the hon. member-he may have missed this in the early part of my remarks-is that I was not going to go through the technical aspects of it. I am dealing with the question of general fairness.
While I am on my feet I will tell him why I think the government has changed its mind on this. In 1984 throughout the campaign the government kept saying how it was going to change the rules of Parliament, reform Parliament, and make it a better institution. It did make some changes. Now it is going back on all that. As the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond pointed out yesterday these changes are not along the lines of the McGrath reforms. They are retrograde steps in most cases and the government has found that its members must stay in Ottawa now. When they were in opposition for 50 years before 1984, with the odd break, they found they could run back and forth to their ridings all the time. Now they have to be here to maintain their majority otherwise they would get defeated in this House and there would be an election in which they would all lose.
When you are at 12 per cent in the polls you do not keep many seats. Even the hon. member for Peace River knows-and he must be quaking in his boots-that he would lose his riding if there were an election tomorrow. So they all stay in Ottawa.
They are down in the polls and they say: "Boy, if we could only get to our ridings we could get up in the polls". They will not because the policies they are pursuing are so bad they cause them to be down in the polls. It is not their presence in Ottawa. It is because their policies are so terrible.
They say: "Well, if we could go out and sell the policies across the country, if we could get out around Canada and tell Canadians what a great job we are doing, they
April 9, 1991

might believe us and maybe we would go up in the polls". They will not. They are going down, and they are staying down, because their policies are so rotten.
We are here exposing those policies day after day and it makes them nervous. So they say: "We do not want our bad policies exposed. We want to spend the time in our ridings instead where at least we can commiserate with the misery we have inflicted on Canadians with our disastrous policies of free trade, GST, high interest rates and all that sort of stuff. Let us shut Parliament down; let us curtail debate; let us limit the right of the opposition to raise subjects of interest. Then we will be all right. Then we will go up in the polls". That is the purpose of these rule changes. That is why they are being done now. Instead of in 1984 or in 1989, they are being brought in in 1991 because they know an election is around the comer. They see how far down they are in the polls and they say: " We have to salvage something from the wreckage of six years of disastrous government."

Mr. Speaker, I certainly listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member from Kingston and the Islands, and I also watched on television the interesting exchange by the member for Winnipeg-Bird's Hill and the member for Surrey-White Rock. I must say that did get more into the atmosphere of debate on something that is pretty important. Those are the rules of this House.
I did subtly remind the former speaker-I have to confess I was here-when we had the last major rules changes in 1969. I think that is when Thumper Macdonald, our present high commissioner in London, got the nickname Thumper. We did have that long debate; it went into the summertime. There were many hours of debate; morning, noon, and night. Then finally the government invoked closure to amend the rules in a more fundamental way than I perceive in these changes.
I have other things I would like to say at some time but I was very interested in the references made by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands. I was here in the House during his leader's speech which was certainly lengthy and did cover points in an arresting way. Frankly I think the opposition is really off base on a lot of its concerns. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands blessed in a government role, would say the same thing the Parliamentary Secretary to the House leader and the member for Peace River would say. I shudder and shake to think what a fellow called Erik Nielsen would do if he

were in this House regarding these rules in view of some of the debates we have had on minor rules changes.

I am very interested as an independent member, and frankly there are going to be more, regardless of the whole thrust of the Elections Act which does not allow independent members to collect money in the same way that members of registered parties collect money. speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in this debate. I do want to say, at the very outset, that the tone of the debate for the last couple of days has been good and has really reflected the kind of attitude the House needs to take to its rule changes.
There are, however, a couple of exceptions. The first day was entirely wasted by having the Speaker read the motion before this House. Members could have better
used that time to discuss the issues that are so important to us.
I am a little disappointed that the member for Kingston and the Islands chose not to discuss at length and in detail some of the changes. Having worked with him at great length over the last few months on these rule changes, I know he has a very clear understanding of not only of the rules as proposed, but of the implications of those rules and an understanding of the tradition which has been part of the process that has brought us to where we are today in the House of Commons.
It has been a fascinating process to go through these negotiations in the last few months, to look at a number of Standing Orders and to come up with a package which I think is a significant package, a package which is good for the whole House. It is not a package designed, as the hon. members opposite would have you believe, to protect a government on the run. It is anything but that. It is is consistent with the McGrath reforms. It builds on those reforms and brings some of them up to date to face the reality that we live with today.
It is consistent with some of the work begun by Tom Lefebvre as chairman of another committee on rule changes back in 1980-81. That was my first experience with rule changes. I was privileged as a new member of this house to be a member of that committee and found it a very enlightening experience and a great opportunity to get a bit of an understanding of the traditions of this House.
I think the rule changes we are dealing with here in the House today are consistent with those traditions.
There are about four particular elements that I want to address in my remarks today. I want to begin by looking at the changes to the committee process. I begin there because, for me, that is one of the most interesting and exciting elements of the House of Commons procedures and processes. I begin there because one of my favourite times as a member was the time that I spent on committees.
I was a member of the McGrath task force when I thought that committees, for the first time, were given powers and opportunities which they never had before. When I was a member of a committee in opposition, the only things we could work on were those items referred
April 9, 1991

to us by a minister of the Crown. We, as a committee, never had the opportunity to discuss anything that was controversial or anything that would have in any way pushed the government.
This government changed that significantly with the McGrath task force by allowing committees to become self-starting, by allow committees freedom and latitude to work within their subject areas to develop policy ideas and to develop a process that could have an influence on the government process in this country.
Out of that flowed two very significant elements. One was that standing committees would be self-starting; with the ability to move, to act and to explore. The other was to put in place legislative committees. Those legislative committees were to, at that point, deal strictly with legislation, to deal with it in a technical way and to accept the fact that the House had already adopted, in principle, the legislation that was referred to the legislative committee.
That is where McGrath started. It is where McGrath put forward a proposal which was accepted by this House.
Unfortunately, since that time a couple of things have happened. The legislative committees, not in all cases but in some cases, began to view themselves, not as legislative committees, but as standing committees.
They began to fuzz the two lines that were to exist between these committees and try to get them both to function in the same way. It undermined a very fundamental part of what I thought the McGrath task force was trying to establish.
The McGrath task force had recommended that the number of standing committees be reduced and that the membership of those committees be small, preferably around eight members. Since then we have gone from the 17 or 18 committees that the McGrath task force recommended, to some 21 to 23 today.
We have also gone from the majority of committees being eight or nine members to 14 members. As a result, we have once again undermined some of the fundamental elements of the McGrath task force.
That brings me to the changes we have here. We asked that the committees be developed into five envelopes. The committees remain. We do not change them.
Government Orders
However, they are gathered into five envelopes. Each of those envelopes has a consistency which flows through it-a thread of common interest. Whether it is an economic interest, a human resources interest or a natural resources interest dealing with things like oil, gas and forestry, there is a common thread there.
The reason for that is to pick up on what the McGrath task force tried to accomplish: To develop an expertise in our standing committees that would serve as a resource for both this House and for the government in the development of policy or legislation that would affect this country.
I think that by bringing us back to this envelope process, we encourage the concentration and the development of that expertise. We do not in any way change the membership rights which members enjoy under the McGrath task force. In fact, it is the member who, under these proposals, continues to have the say over his or her substitutes on a particular committee. Within an envelope dealing with that substitution list submitted by a member, it is very easy to make an exchange.
Consistent with McGrath, we have tried to bring the legislative committees it back to what was originally suggested: Legislative committees will be legislative committees. They will not try to act as standing committees. They will not try to be something they were not designed to be. They will look at technical witnesses and they will meet with them. Technical witnesses may include members of a department, people who work for a department, lawyers who are familiar with the subject area, or interest groups that have a technical response to a bill. The fundamental goal of the McGrath task force was to see that those legislative committees would accept that the House had already dealt with that bill in principle. There is a thread there.
There is another important aspect in this rule change package. Right now, if the House were to decide to send a specific issue to a standing committee, for example, but there was not consent to do so, the House would have no choice but to refer the bill, or the subject matter of it, to a legislative committee even though there may be widespread support on all sides of the House to send it to the specific standing committee, or a special committee. One of the rule changes we provided for in this particular package, is that now by vote the House can decide to

April 9, 1991
Government Orders
send a bill or an issue to a special committee, to a standing committee, or to a legislative committee. This is very consistent with the kind of goals the McGrath task force was trying to accomplish.
There is one exception in the area of committees which caused me some concern, and I know will have caused some concern to other members familiar with the work of McGrath. One of the things we had recommended during the McGrath work was that parliamentary secretaries not be part of standing committees. Mr. Speaker, we did that based on the experience that all of us had come through in that period. From 1980 to 1984, it was the government which directed what issues any particular committee would or could discuss. When an issue was before a standing committee, the parliamentary secretary started acting like a policeman or a director. He or she had tremendous control over that committee. As a result, members reacted by saying they did not want parliamentary secretaries on committees.
Since the McGrath reforms, what has happened is that opposition critics who are expert in a given subject area are members and active participants in the committees. But on the government side the one individual who is not a member of cabinet, yet has the most experience with a particular subject area, bill, or issue, the parliamentary secretary, is excluded from the process.
So, Mr. Speaker, we have come full circle. We have now said that we saw where McGrath was going; we understood what McGrath was trying to accomplish at the time; but it was not working. It was not working because the committee was being robbed of an individual who was a tremendous resource to the committee in terms of information, in terms of access to the department, and all that is going on within that particular department.
We have now come to the point where we feel it is time to put the parliamentary secretaries back into the committee, to give them an opportunity to build bridges between the committee and the department, and the department and the committee. I hope this will fulfil the very goals the McGrath task force set out to accomplish, which was to give backbenchers in the House of Commons an opportunity through the committee process to develop policies, legislation, and direction on any issue that this country may be faced with.
I referred very briefly to the requests of McGrath to reduce the size of our committees from 14 members to 8. We have renewed that request in this package. We have not done it by changing the rules and by restricting in our Standing Orders the sizes of committees. We did not do that for a reason which is very simple. It is something we want negotiated and discussed by the members of this House. My own experience was that when I have been a member of a small committee, that committee worked well. It built a relationship within itself that often ended up with a unanimous report which then was reflected in the legislation of the day.
Therefore, we have once again put the request to members on all sides of this House that they seriously consider reducing those committees that now have memberships of 14 members, and reducing them to eight. It is an option of the House. It is not something the government has any intention to direct, or wants to direct. It is a process we hope the members themselves will develop and see the opportunity that we think exists.
The last matter I want to mention about committees is the question of televising committee hearings. That has been an issue of controversy in the House and for good reason. There are some very strongly held feelings on both sides of this House. For example, I am concerned that when the television cameras came into the Chamber-I was not here before-one of the things that began to happen and is part of our everyday experience here now is that many of us play to the cameras when participating in debate. We do not play to the audience, or talk to the people here in the Chamber, or to the Chair. We play to the cameras. As a result it changes our behaviour.
What happens if we go into a committee environment and the same thing happens there? The one area in our parliamentary process that has been very active, very influential, what if it too becomes another stage? Then we have a problem.
Nevertheless, we must recognize that we are in a new world today. It is unfair to allow print media to have full access to committees and yet not allow electronic media
April 9, 1991

the same access. We shut out radio and television. We have to recognize that reality.
That is why in these rules there is now a change to develop experimental guidelines for the televising and radio linkage of committee hearings. We use the word "experimental" because it is very fundamental. It is very important. We have to build an experience together and we have to decide on a type of system that will allow the committees to function to their maximum ability, yet provide, as much as possible, equal access to all media, electronic or print.
The second thing that I want to touch on, briefly, is the calendar. That has been one of the areas which has received significant media attention. We have heard all sorts of arguments about it. The proposal in this particular package is that we move to the three and one formula, where the House would sit approximately three weeks and then it would not sit for one week. That time could be used for one of two things: first, members could return to their ridings to meet with their constituents, to hold public meetings, private meetings, whatever they choose to do; or, second, that time could be used for committee work.
I heard yesterday the member from Hamilton going on and on about how this was running away from responsibility. He had no problem being here in the House of Commons. He could be here Friday. He could be here Monday. Therefore this was a gross example of a government trying to duck and run.
Mr. Speaker, I have to tell you as a member that was sitting in this House listening to that speech, I was very much offended by it. Why was I offended? Because I cannot travel to my riding in two or three or even six hours. To get to my constituency takes me 12 hours. If I want to be back in my riding to hold meetings on Saturday morning, I have to leave here Thursday night. If I am going to be here Monday, I have to leave Sunday night.
So, Mr. Speaker, you can see very quickly for someone like myself, who lives in a northern and a western riding, why this kind of formula has a great deal of appeal. I can then stay here through that three-week period. I can focus and dedicate my time to the work of the House, committees or whatever particular role I may have at that moment, but then I can take a week-and in fact, if you take in the weekends, which gives you a little bit
Government Orders
more time-I can go home and do some concentrated constituency work, listening to my people, gathering their concerns and bringing them back with me and hopefully have those reflected in the debates and the issues before this House.
I was offended when I heard a member, who can be on a plane and probably in his riding in two or three hours, or even jump in a car and be there in five hours, tell me that I am neglecting my duties and my responsibilities and I am somehow ducking the issue by asking that instead of giving me a weekend, that I get from time to time a week to work in my riding.
Mr. Speaker, you are signalling that my time is about to expire. It is unfortunate because I am just beginning my remarks.
There are a number of things that flow from those changes. There is the reduction in the budget days from six debating days to four. There is the reduction in the throne speech from eight to six days. There is the reduction in the allotted days from 25 to 20. All of those flow from the calendar, not because we are trying to limit debate. If I were to buy the logic of the opposition, then to have the perfect democracy we would sit 365 days. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, their whole argument is that democracy is based on the number of days that we sit. So we are going to go for perfection in Canada. We will sit 365 days.
The problem is, Mr. Speaker, that if you look at what happens in the opposition benches, they are on a roster system. One-third of their members at any one time are back in their ridings. They are not here working in the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, my time has expired. I wish I had more time to continue with my arguments. I believe very strongly this package is consistent with the work began by Tom Lefebvre and is consistent with the reforms brought in by the McGrath task force. This is a package that is designed to help all members of the House, whether they are on the opposition benches or the government benches.
It is not a Draconian package. It is not fascist as we heard it described. It is a fair package and it is one that I am very comfortable defending in any forum, including the one where it is going to have the most impact, here in the House of Commons.

April 9, 1991
Government Orders

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed the parliamentary secretary's speech, as I thought I would. As the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-Langley indicated, it was not a history lesson. I am sorry that he did not enjoy my history lesson. I thought he might have found it helpful to fit these rule changes into the context, particularly when I was quoting most extensively in my speech from his former leader, Mr. Diefenbaker. I am surprised he was disappointed in that.
The hon. member for Peace River in his speech talked about the wonders of the rule changes and particularly the change that allows the one week off for the member to go to his riding. I think he misconstrued the remarks of the hon. member for Hamilton West, and I admit it was open to this misconstruction yesterday. But the point the hon. member for Hamilton West was making so effectively was that he did not object to members having a week off, his objection was to the cutback in the number of days of sitting.
Surely the parliamentary secretary, who was after all instrumental in discussing these matters, I presume, with his boss the government House leader, could have said: "Look, the opposition has trouble cutting the number of days from 174 or 175 to 134. Maybe another way to do this is to sit an additional three-week period. Give another 15 sitting days in the summer, at some other time of year." But what the government did was say, keep the holidays we now have, let us add to them.
I use the word "holiday" advisedly, because like the hon. member for Peace River, when I go to my riding I work quite hard. I spend time there and I spend many hours working there. I think most hon. members do exactly that. So I do not call it a holiday but it is a time away from working in this place. The public, naturally, regards members as working only when they are in Ottawa, it seems, but that is not always the case, and I acknowledge that as well as anyone else.
If the government was serious in its suggestion that it really wanted to give members time to be in their ridings, why did it simply deduct sitting days from the calendar and take an extra week off here and there? Why did it not add another three weeks of sitting, in September or August or July, or January which now is free of sittings,
and continue at least something close to the number of sitting days? Why did it reduce the sitting days so much in order to achieve its end? Because we could have had three weeks of sitting in January and another week or two before the scheduled resumption date in February. All that could have been done quite easily, but the government chose not to. They simply reduced. Could the parliamentary secretary answer that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yes. I am very pleased to answer the concerns of my hon. friend from Kingston and the Islands.
He will know from several of the meetings that he and I had with Mark Houlton from our office, who worked so hard on this package.
As a government, we put forward two proposals; one was to sit Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, and the House not to sit on Fridays and keep roughly the same parliamentary calendar as exists today; or the second proposal which was to go with the three and one option.
What the hon. member should recall is that it was the request and the feedback from the opposition members which indicated they preferred the three and one.
There is a difference between what is said in private and what is said in public. I want to be very specific and I do not want to accuse anyone. I am not saying that the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands supported the three and one proposal. I want to be very clear about that. What I am saying is that the feedback from the opposition benches indicated the one that had the best consensus on both sides of the House-
Most palatable.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Most palatable-that is the word I will accept-was the three and one proposal. That is why we chose to go with it. It was not an arbitrary decision of the government; it was part of the discussions and negotiations that had been going on for months.
I am glad the hon. member asked the question as it gives me an opportunity to put on record the facts of what really happened in terms of the calendar changes.

I appreciate the hon. member's response, Mr. Speaker. I think he stated it correctly. He asked which of the two we preferred and we said that we did not like either, but if we had to chose we would take
April 9, 1991

Government Orders
this one. That is what we said. It was the more palatable Richmond pointed out yesterday, but, by and large, we of the two.	can agree with the package.
What I have indicated, and what we have indicated throughout, is that we were not in favour of reducing the number of sitting days of this House. I hope he has got that message.
To put the negotiations in context, I think it is fair for the hon. member to know, and he may want to comment on this, that when the government makes a proposal to change rules without going through the usual committee routine of coming up with changes, as happened with the Private Members' Business changes which the government has included in this package and which were the result of an all-party committee meeting and which were unanimously recommended to this House by the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. Even the New Democratic member sitting on that committee agreed with the changes that were proposed. We have made no amendments to all those changes that have been proposed. We agree with those changes. They were the result of all-party work in that committee.
Had the parliamentary secretary gone to a committee, I suggest, as I said in my remarks, we might have achieved more consensus. But what the government does when it says: "We are going to change the rules", is say to the opposition: "You can negotiate with us to the extent that we are willing to bend but, in the end, with our majority, we are going to do what we like."
What happens, as an opposition, is that we are put in a position of trying to get the best deal we possibly can, but knowing that if we do not try to do that the government will go and do exactly what it wants anyway and then we will really get kicked in the teeth.
What we did, in the course of these talks, is try to soften the blow that the government was delivering in the form of these rule changes, to get the best package that we could live with by indicating our areas of strongest disagreement, of strongest dissent so the government would know where it is going to find itself in difficulty.
Does the hon. member for Peace River not realize that when a government starts negotiating on rule changes, something that is fundamental in this House, is negotiating from a position of tremendous strength and that the opposition has very few levers with which to play? Does he not realize that those negotiations would result in answers and in responses that perhaps would lead the government to think it has agreement when it does not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my friend was obviously a successful lawyer in his private life before coming to this institution. He makes a bad argument sound pretty convincing and pretty good.
The truth is what has happened in this case. We start out, as a government, putting forward a proposal. We put that proposal on the table and we discuss it with the opposition parties. We change that package and that proposal to the point where it is hardly recognizable. We take that package and bring it into the House. But what happens then? The opposition takes the things that it was not successful in changing and chooses to highlight them and oppose the final result.
Members do not mention the fact that we, as the government, have made significant changes. I am sorry, in fairness you are right, the hon. member did say that. What they do, and I think the House leader for the government put it very well yesterday, is they want to have their cake and eat it too. They want to go through all of the discussions, all of the negotiations, get all of the changes they can and then, in the end, oppose the package. They call it things like fascist, Draconian and all sorts of negative terms when, in fact, it was a very, very effective and good negotiation process which I think resulted in some very positive changes. I am not trying to take credit for those. I am quite prepared to give the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands a great deal of credit because he did make a number of suggestions. He and Mr. Yanover put forward a number of really positive suggestions which we have incorporated into the rule changes and, I think, have strengthened the package.
Our amendment indicates those areas where we feel It is unfortunate that once again the opposition men-the government is wrong. We have some reservations in tality, rather than support the package, is trying to other places, as the hon. member for Cape Breton-East manipulate us as a government into a position where we

April 9, 1991
Government Orders
are forced to use closure to put what I think is a very good package through this House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise and add my perspective to the particular changes that are being proposed by the government, some of which are certainly of interest and some of which were long overdue. I personally would love to see much more free voting on the part of members so that they do not have to be following the Whip's line all the time.
That is something that I have found very hard to accept. In fact, I found it very galling at certain moments in the course of my last two mandates in this House.
In speaking to the rules of order of change in the House, I think that if they were passed as they have been presented by the government, they would permanently alter Parliament as Canadians have come to know it. I think that Canadians have come to be much more aware and sensitized to the House through what Mr. Warren has explained to them as he puts on our television tube the procedures of the House.
I think that has been very important in helping people to understand what is fairly complex as a procedure.
I see one of my colleagues from Alberta across the floor. I recall our coming in here together and doing a bill on chips and costs. We all had difficulty learning how the House operated. We in this House had difficulty learning and adapting. We did not know we were supposed to be partisan in this House. A colleague from the Conservative bench helped me as I was trying to address a bill that I knew very little about at that given moment.
I think I came out with some enlightened observations, both from my own side, that of the opposition, and the government side. I think that that is what it would allow us if there were more free votes in this House: To have and to be able to express joint and common views which we share that do not necessarily require the kind of party line vote in areas that are quite diverse in what we address in this House.

So, the changes this government is proposing to the Standing Orders are a further proof that the Prime
Minister is trying to dismantle our national institutions, as he just did with the CBC. It makes absolutely no sense! The new rules undermine the legitimate role of Parliament, that is to confront the government with its responsibilities. The proposed changes are intended to stifle the Parliament of Canada.
The government proposal relinquishes altogether the notion of consensus between parties in this House. The McGrath reforms, and the earlier Lefebvre reforms, as well as the 1969 amendments, were all based upon full ranging debates with a view to reaching a consensus in a spirit of co-operation. Parliament is the latest victim of a dictatorial decision-making process that is what my colleague from Kingston and the Islands was discussing with the member opposite.

While some say that the Conservative government lacks direction, purpose and a clear vision of Canada, I do not say that I particularly share that point of view in this Parliament. I would argue quite the opposite.
I would say that while it appears to be bungling its way through almost every issue that faces this country, the Conservatives in my view have a very clear agenda that seeks to fundamentally change the structures and the institutions of this country and not in the best interests of the unity or well-being of this country, or in the forward agenda of Canada for Canadians: men, women and children to be distinct on the global map.
That has been the hidden agenda. That is the forward agenda, and that is what it does when it dismantles the institutions like the institutions of this House. The proposed changes to the rules are just that other step of closing down Canada.
I would call this the dismantling of the strongest national institutions, Parliament and the House of Commons. Parliament to me is a sacred trust. If it is to be altered, it must not be done in a way that is in the best interest of the government of the day, but what is in the best interest of the people of Canada, Parliament's shareholders.
I speak knowing that we are going to be the government of today tomorrow, and I say that it is not good for us as Liberals as it is not good for the Conservatives.
April 9, 1991

It is bad decision making on the part of this Parliament to allow this kind of dictatorial decision making.

Under the proposed changes, the House would sit eight weeks less every year and there would be fewer days to debate the budget and the throne speech. The number of opposition days where motions on sensitive political issufes can be debated would also be reduced.

The government may argue that it has a majority mandate from the people to govern, but I would argue that the government did not put its full agenda before Canadians during the last election. I heard my hon. colleague-who is about the walk out of the House-say that the government's agenda has always been frustrated. I would suggest that the government's agenda was not always forward in the course of a political election.
For example, did the Prime Minister say that if elected-come on there, Don Blenkam, I ask you-did the government say that if elected it would eliminate 50 per cent of our national railway? Did it say that?
No, no.

Did the Conservatives say they would close CBC stations from coast to coast, from one end of this country to the other, and dismantle that institution?
Did they say that their government would introduce a new major sales tax on everything from reading, intellectual property, the right to knowledge, to taxi cabs and to one yoghurt that they had to go and-
Yes, they did.
No, they did not. Did he say his government would introduce-
And unanimously too.

Never mind. That is not so, I do not believe. The answer is no, no and no. Let us remember that the role of the Official Opposition is today in a working democracy, something perhaps they have forgotten about. A democracy only works when there is opposition. It does not work with the tyranny of the majority.
I quote a man of great stature and influence in the business world, as a deputy minister within the structure
Government Orders
of the government that makes it work, and as a minister of this House, the former Mitchell Sharp, who said that the role of the opposition is to play the role of the defence lawyer, to be sure that the government proves to the public every point and every policy beyond a shadow of a doubt.
I would say the government under its new rules will not allow the opposition to play that role and to hold the government to account, for with less sitting time, shorter debates, restraints and restrictions of powers of legislative committees, the government will become even more tyrannical. Perhaps it did not realize that. However, that is the end result, the bottom line.
The government, since 1988, has known the depth and breadth of the unpopularity of its economic agenda. Its political agenda has not been popular. Look at the polls and then tell me I am wrong. As a result, it has short-circuited parliamentary debate on important issues, in large measure through the use of closure, the cutting off of parliamentary debate, both in the House and in the Senate.
One former Conservative minister, and I think he was quite well respected in this House at that point, Erik Nielsen, said and I quote: "The procedure of closure had been repugnant to the Canadian people. My own personal view is that never in parliamentary debate should there be a muzzling of free debate." That is a citation from him. Yet the government has used closure on an unprecedented scale, especially since 1988.
On the second day this House sat after the 1988 election, the government introduced closure to ram through the free trade agreement, even though a majority of Canadians, 57 per cent, had voted for parties opposed to the trade deal.
Then closure was used at three different stages on Bill C-21 under which the government will eliminate the federal contribution to unemployment insurance, thus abandoning its responsibility to job reduction-
Oh, oh.

You know, you are such a nice guy. Why don't you just button the lip and listen to what I have to say, and then you can argue afterward.
Closure was used twice on the notorious clawback bill which taxed back our senior's pensions, twice on the GST and twice on the bill to privatize Petro-Canada. In total, the Conservatives have invoked closure or time

April 9, 1991
Government Orders
allocation no fewer than 21 times in 29 months since the 1988 election.
The Conservatives invented closure under Sir Robert Borden in 1913 to get passage of their naval aid bill. It was strongly opposed by Liberal opposition leader Sir Wilfred Laurier, who, during the 1913 debate on the closure proposal said that he was going to feel much more comfortable in a defeat at the polls, rather than using closure, because he felt it was so Draconian, so anti-democratic, so far from any of the principles that he supported, that he went the whole way. I quote what he said: "Heaven is my witnesses that I would rather stand here today defeated and in opposition by that appeal to the people than stand over there in office by the power of the gag".
I will admit that there may be times when the use of closure or time allocation is justified. From 1913 to 1984 closure was used fewer times in those 71 years than the Conservative use in the last 29 months.
Finding that closure was not sufficient for the government to get its way, we now have more Draconian measures being imposed. The proposal will cut the sitting days of the House of Commons by almost 25 per cent. At a time when this country is facing a constitutional crisis, when there are rising tensions among our aboriginal peoples and international military actions are increasing and there is destabilization in the international world, increasing levels of unemployment, this government is now proposing what they call "holidays". Well, ladies and gentlemen, I would suggest that it is not a holiday to go back to one's riding. It is a responsibility. I see a particular pleasure to go back to your roots, to the people who elected you to hear what they have to say so that you can, in essence, come back here and report.
I would suggest that if you have Friday, Saturday, Sunday and Monday, certainly in most cases that would be adequate. I understand my colleagues from the far west, the far north and the far east would prefer the one week every three weeks. I would say that neither of these proposals is what we have in front of us. We have some other kind of a scheme that lengthens periods that were already on the calendar to even longer periods. It does
not see us come back to this House during enormously long periods of holiday during the summer season.
I would say that the proposals that were made, the options that were given to us were not very palatable, so we picked the lesser of the evils. There certainly was a way in which we did not have to cut from 175 to 134 sitting days. All this is at at time, as I have said, when Canadians are searching for leadership on these issues, when Canadians are listening to hear what their members have to say on these issues of burning concern.
I do not believe that MPs are going to be comfortable with this kind of change. It is a recipe for the rebirth of Canadian values that will not be found in the choking of debate in this House.
As well, it would appear that the government thought longer sitting days would equal the loss of one week a month in sitting time. But tell me, when will the committees meet? When will we meet in legislative committees? Is the government's plan to make them completely inactive or meaningless too, or to hide the issues from public scrutiny to avoid the test of proof beyond a shadow of a doubt?
Checking the government is an obvious task of the opposition party and one I believe the committees of the House have undertaken constructively in areas of legislation, spending and administration. The government always believes its legislation to be good, but that opinion is not always shared by those who are affected by it.
For example, and I can only use the things I have been intimately involved with in this House, the legislation on broadcasting and on copyright, both considered good by the government, had in excess of 50 amendments each. Obviously, these two bills have benefited from committee study and from the amendments which were brought by both sides of the House.
I personally felt that we, the government members and the opposition members, worked constructively together, along with the minister and the parliamentary secretary to improve both of those bills. In scrutinizing the legislation and in prodding the government to take action, we effectively made changes that were very constructive.

April 9, 1991

Other examples of strong committee work involve the review of political appointments to boards, commissions and agencies. I just have to talk about the John Crispo appointment-
Shocking appointment.

-as opposed to the Bill Neville appointment, just to name two, or David Colville to the CRTC. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I do not care what your party party partisanship is. You can be a good strong Conservative, a good strong Liberal, a good strong NDP. As long as you are a considered and thoughtful Canadian, I do not care what your party policy is, but have some knowledge of the dossier which you are considering, the committee on which you are going to sit and have some constructive sense of the role in society. Do not do some of the silly things that this government has done in bad partisan politics. In good partisan politics, I have no objections.
That is why the power of committees to review and to arouse public interest is very important. They do not have that power, as I have said, to rescind or overrule, but they certainly can have a degree of moral suasion when bad appointments have been made and we would hope would make the government more prudent in their nominations.
I would suggest that we try to make committees examine the issue, raise public awareness and, as well, examine every dollar of government expenditure. That is a very important role that opposition must play. It is not easy to find the errors and it is not easy to find the misjudgements, but it is important. We work hard on an opposition bench, with very small staff, to find those errors. That is why we have to be in this House as well to carry out that responsibility. We do spot checking, as you know Mr. Speaker when you were on committee, and you did it very effectively as well.
I believe it could be said that we do have a salutary effect on government when it knows we are on the outlook for waste, for inappropriate and unbalanced regional spending or non-spending. For those kind of extravagances, I could allude to the Department of Communications and its minister, but I will not bother the House at this particular moment. I have done it at other stages.
After all, it is the people's money. I think we have to be more frugal and more prudent with that money than we are with our own money and our own pocket-book.
Government Orders
That is a commitment that every member takes and should observe when they come to this House, and it is their responsibility.
I think that we have to look at government administration of its departments and its agencies. By the very nature of things, we are the receivers of complaints from public servants, public people and taxpayers. I hear from the film makers, the broadcasters, the artists, the performers, and the business people. As well, I hear from people about the ordinary problems in my riding: employment, pensions, all kinds of serious concerns from people who are dissatisfied, from refugees and immigration, et cetera. It is our job to be in the riding, hear about these issues related to our portfolio and related to our ordinary people and bring them back and ask questions in this House.
Recent investigations by the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture involving the National Arts Centre, Telefilm Canada, the National Gallery and the CBC have been very important. How committees undertake their work I think is equally important.
Mr. Speaker, you have advised me that I have very little time left. I want to talk about just two other things. One is the importance of opposition days, that we are able on opposition days to take initiatives, to discuss issues that go beyond partisan politics and look at societal issues of concern. We had a marvellous debate in this House on violence against women. Even though it was brought before this House by the Liberal Party, that was not the point. Every member on all sides who participated added to the understanding and awareness of the community out there through an opposition day of this nature.
The development of human resources, education, job training, research and development, agriculture and fishing were very important. That is why opposition days must be maintained, because they are vital. Losing those 40 sitting days will also require us to reduce those opposition days, the number of question periods, our debates on the budget and on the throne speech and certainly on other aspects of our daily work.
In summation, I would just like to make the following points. There is no protection in the simple title of democracy. Even the best intentioned rulers in any kind of a democratic society, if they are left unchecked, they become very autocratic. I would remind hon. members

April 9, 1991

that Lord Acton said that "power tends to corrupt and absolute power corrupts absolutely".
I finish with a quote from Benjamin Disraeli who says that "the function of the opposition is essentially one of criticism". It is critical that we allow for the kinds of sitting days-just find other opportunities and other ways-which allow the House to expose the issues, which allow constant probing, and which allow us to play the role that we were elected to play in this House.
I thank you very much Mr. Speaker and I hope that the public will be aroused enough that it will let the government know that this is not acceptable; we must have consultation and it must go to a committee, it cannot be done arbitrarily as we plan to do it today.
